stories.title_en: Setting Up Fake Ingots to Swindle Country Farmers

paragraphs.en: There was once a man, a farmer by birth. He worked his fields hard, ate and dressed simply, and was terribly tight with money, so his household was fairly well off. A con man from out of town came to this district, learning that the farmer was greedy and dull-witted. He found out which day the farmer would be plowing a certain field and buried two fake yuanbao ingots there ahead of time, weighing a hundred taels in total. While the farmer was hard at his plowing, the crook deliberately wandered the hillside nearby, pretending to search left and right. The farmer asked, “What are you looking for here?” The con man said, “I am looking for something. What is it to you?” The farmer had to keep quiet. The con man then examined one tree, then another, like a man who had lost something. The farmer spoke again: “You are a strange one—what do you mean by going all over the hill checking trees?” The con man said, “I will not hide it from you. Years ago my late father was captured by roving bandits and joined their gang. Later he came into so much silver that he could not carry it alone, so he buried it in various places and left an account book recording the spots, meaning to come back for it—but he died, poor man. Now I have come with the book to find the one under a tree here, and I cannot tell which tree it is. Lucky for me you are here. Come help me look; if we find it, I do not mind sharing some with you.” The farmer took his hoe and searched with him. Sure enough, under one tree they found two yuanbao. The con man feigned great delight and said, “If we have found this one, all the other spots can be found. I am truly willing to share it with you—only we have no hammer or chisel here.” He went on, “I have nowhere to keep this silver. Why not go to your house? Help me finish the search, and I will thank you with several ingots. What do you say?” The farmer said, “Fine with me. But you and I have never met. If you suddenly start coming and going at my house, will people not grow suspicious?” The con man said, “We should say I am some relative or old friend.” The farmer said, “I have it. I had a brother-in-law, my wife’s brother, who was sold at six or seven to a merchant from outside the province, and nothing has been heard of him since. We will pass you off as my wife’s brother, come back to see his sister and her husband. Why not?” And he told the con man, one by one, the names and appearance of his wife’s parents.

He led him home and called his wife out to meet her "brother." When she saw him, she asked, "Why does my brother’s face look nothing like mine?" The con man answered, "I went away to another province; the local fortune there is different, so I do not resemble you." She asked again, "What was my father’s name, and what did he look like? My mother’s name, and her looks?" The con man answered without a mistake. She asked, "And my uncle—his name and looks?" He answered, "I left home as a small child; I remember only my parents, not my uncle." The wife believed him. She killed a chicken and cooked fresh fish, laying out a fine feast for her "brother." The farmer’s brothers and the rest of the family each gave him a generous meal in turn. The con man said to his "brother-in-law," "I need some loose silver for spending. Let me take fifteen or sixteen taels from your house for my sundry expenses." The farmer then took out more than ten taels of his own genuine silver and gave it to the con man.

A few days later, the con man checked the ledger with his brother-in-law: there were still over a dozen gold ingots hidden in a chapel on such-and-such a hill. The chapel was empty. The brother-in-law packed two boxes of food and drink and carried them there on a pole. Two accomplices the con man had posted in the chapel were already waiting; they bound the farmer backward against a pillar. The two drew ox-tail knives and repeatedly threatened to kill him. The con man pretended to plead for him: "My brother-in-law has treated me generously, and I have eaten plenty of his family's chicken and fish. Do not kill my sister's husband." The three crooks ate the food and left. The farmer cried out to heaven but got no answer; he had no door into the earth. Not until the afternoon of the next day did a herdboy pass by. The farmer shouted for help, was untied, and made his way home. His wife asked, "Why are you only back today? Why didn't your brother come back?" The farmer answered, "Don't speak of him. Don't speak of him." To this day, when someone has been swindled, the common saying is, "Don't speak of him."

Not long ago, a man in Jiangyuan was swindled by a con man in exactly the same way. His wife was sharp: she had the silver ingot chiseled open at once and saw it was tin. They bound the crook, beat him, forced a written confession out of him, and only then let him go. Had his wife not been so clever, he would have met the same fate as the earlier farmer. To regret it only then—would that not have been too late?

Note: This farmer worked himself hard, scrimped on food and clothing, and so grew rich—a fortunate man. Why did he let greed drive him into the crooks’ cage, to lose his money and be shamed, ending up less wise than the woman of Jiangyuan? But in these latter days deceit flourishes and villains appear in a hundred shapes. Lately “dropped-bundle” thieves have cheated a great many people, and in the country between the Yangzi and the Huai there is another trick, called “the tug-and-drop,” that is even harder to guard against: the thief only has to ask you one question—answer him once and you are spellbound. It is sorcery, and it has harmed even more people. Have the ways of the world and the hearts of men really sunk to this? Coming across these stories, I have set them down in full as a warning to all who travel.

stories.title_en: Accepting Bleached Counterfeit Silver at the Maozhou Fair

paragraphs.en: Qian Tianguang was a man of Anhai in Fujian. Once he bought loom-woven cloth and took it to sell at the Medicine King Fair in Maozhou, Shandong. The fair ran from the fifteenth of the fourth month to the twenty-fifth, and goods from all over the empire were unloaded and traded there. There were no brokers to set a middle price; buyer and seller dealt directly with each other.

A con man came to buy cloth, paying with washed silver. Each ingot weighed five taels; genuine silver was mixed in with the fake, identical in color. The con man first presented fine-thread silver for testing. Guang hammered and chiseled them and found nothing amiss. After testing over ten ingots, all uniform, Guang said, "No need to hammer and chisel any more." The con man then brought out the washed silver to settle the payment: over six hundred taels in total, of which only about a hundred were genuine fine-thread silver—the rest was all fake. The silver was handed over, and the cloth was carried away. Guang packed his bags, hired a mule cart with fellow townsfolk, and went straight to Linqing to buy goods for the return trip. When he took out the silver, it was all fake. Regret was useless by then, but Guang did not take it too hard. He only said, "I was the one who took this bait at this fair. Let it end with me; may no other traveling merchant suffer the same." People marveled at his magnanimity: after such a great fall, he was bound to rise high. The crook may have gotten away with several hundred taels, but Heaven’s principle is clear—his descendants will not prosper. Fake silver is found everywhere in the empire, so I record this as a precaution for those who come after: do not repeat Qian Tianguang’s mistake. Observation: Of all the traps a merchant faces, fake silver is the hardest to guard against; you must grasp the general method before you can spot it. In the autumn of the renzi year, I came across a little booklet in a bookshop that explained how to tell true silver from false, very clearly. I transcribe it here for traveling merchants to read, so that fake silver is plain the moment it meets the eye. I give a few of its points below:

A yuanbao is the "original treasure" as it comes directly from the mine pits. Today, the government's shipments of tax silver are likewise melted and refined to high purity, just like pit-washed silver, and cast into yuanbao. In common speech, this is called "round treasure."
Pine-grain (songwen) is the same as fine-thread (xisi); both are silver of full fineness.
Shaken-thread (yaosi): the purity is not yet high enough. The silver is poured in and shaken by hand until threads form—hence the name "shaken-thread."
Water-thread (shuisi), also called dry-thread (gansi): all grades from seven-tenths to nine-and-a-half tenths fine are collectively known as water-thread.
Drawn-thread (huasi) is water-silk. It is poured out as a mass without distinct threads, so an iron awl is used to draw thread-like lines on its surface—hence the name "drawn-thread."
Blown-thread (chuisi) is water-thread of nine-tenth fineness. Once the silver is poured, the maker holds a blowpipe in his mouth and blows it into threads—hence the name "blown-thread."

Sucked-thread (xisi): wet paper is laid over the top with a hole in the middle; silver is poured through the hole and drawn into threads—hence the name. Nowadays, people use iron foil instead, again with a central hole, pouring silver through to draw it into threads. This technique covers fineness from seven-tenths up to nine-and-a-half; the latter can pass for pure silver.

Tea-flower (chahua): take nine qian of fine silver and one qian of lead, put them in the furnace pan without a speck of niter, and pour it out openly. A pale base is packed into the feet, and the silver is then poured in so the lead does not show, while coarse threads form of themselves—hence “tea-flower.”

Tripod silver (dingyin) is mercury silver, also called quicksilver. Take five qian of fine silver and five and a half qian of mercury in an iron tripod; heat until the inside glows red. Remove it, let it cool, then extract the silver: you get only one tael, with five fen of mercury recoverable. It can be hammered into shape or cast into cakes. Silver leaf is pasted on the outside, lightly sprinkled with ink to mask its overly white appearance. It can also be made into wine vessels and various ornaments, drawn into silver wire much like fine thread, though slightly greener in hue. There is also "barefoot" mercury silver: three qian of fine silver, two qian of copper wire, and five and a half qian of mercury, treated similarly—melted, poured, and extracted. It cannot be worked further and resembles water-silk. To identify mercury silver: the base color is soft, and the silver leaf pasted on top differs from the barefoot variety's hue; reddish yet soft, it never achieves the aged look of water-silk. This lore has been passed down since ancient times. Those who fabricated this silver to deceive others amassed fortunes of thousands, yet their descendants proved unworthy, and the family soon fell into decline. Harming the public to build a fortune never endures.

Copper-core: copper is set around the four sides and silver is poured over it, hiding the copper inside—this is what they call "copper." You can examine the threads, but they will never shine as brightly as those of fine silver. If the threads are coarse and stiff, suspect it and chisel it open to reveal the copper.

Iron-bits (tiesui): broken iron is placed inside first, and then molten silver is poured over it so that it takes the iron in evenly, encasing it in the middle. Even the lowest grade still comes out at nine-tenths purity, and at nine-and-a-half tenths it even shows fine silver threads.
Some use bits of copper as described earlier, calling it "baoxiao silver." The lowest grade is still ninety percent fine; at ninety-five percent there are silk threads, at ninety percent none.

Chaozai copper: Put one tael of copper and three fen of silver into the furnace. Add white arsenic, drawing it in like niter, and pour it into the center. Remove the piece and trim off three or four fen from the four sides; return the center to the furnace to melt again. Repeat this clipping and melting several times. Then take silver powder ground extremely fine in a bowl, pound sour-arsenic herb to extract its juice, add three fen of borax, and boil them together in a small pot. Next, add the initial three fen of silver powder into the herb juice. Place the copper into the pot, stir with chopsticks, remove it, and wash away the herb juice with clean water until the color is very white. Someone asked, "You used only three fen of silver in the copper initially, then another three fen of silver powder—how does that make silver appear on the outside?" The answer was: "Of all the world's treasures, gold and silver are the most precious. If you do not first melt three fen of silver into the copper, boiling it later with silver powder will never work. With the first three fen of silver inside, the subsequent boiling with silver powder naturally bonds." That is why making fake silver is popularly called "the immortals' art." To spot this copper, examine the silver color: it is a dead-fish white, lacking any blue-white sheen. Then inspect the feet, which come in two varieties—some dotted with rouge, others with mineral pigment. Judge it by the dotted feet and the dead-fish white, and the true versus the false will be plain.

Bleached (piaobai): silver is melted and poured just like fine-thread, except that because it is poured while extremely hot, the walls come out thin. Next, the bottom is removed and only the thin top is kept. White copper is poured into the middle with no wall of its own; the saved top is fitted over it; silver foil is joined underneath; and the whole piece is soldered together. Its base is then beaten with a dross hammer until it is indistinguishable from a genuine wind-pot casting. Even chiseling it open cannot tell them apart. To recognize it: during soldering, the fire burns away the natural bluish sheen and leaves a dead-fish white—hence the name "bleached." Judge it by this, and the difference is crystal clear.

The method for refining cake silver: for every qian of lead used, melt in one fen of copper. For one tael of nine-tenths silver, use one tael of lead; for eight-tenths, two taels; for seven-tenths, three taels. Pack charcoal into the furnace within an ash-lined hearth and fan the fire gently until the lead melts. Afterward, fan vigorously; when oil beads grow as large as beans, cover the pot and remove it immediately—this yields ninety-five percent purity. If you wait until golden flowers blaze before removing it, a crust forms on top called "cloth-heart cake" or "scorched-heart cake." Below lie crab-eyes and returning pearls, with both faces white: this indicates pine-grain silver at full fineness.
A nine-tenths purity ingot also appears white upon removal from the mold: its top surface bears a chicken-claw texture, while the base below is likewise white.
Eight-tenths cake comes out of the furnace slightly black; it must be rubbed with fine polishing sand to turn white. There are flea-spot marks on top; snip it open and it is slightly white inside.
Seven-tenths cake comes out of the furnace ink-black; it too must be rubbed with sand and washed with salted plums to turn white, and the snipped edge carries a reddish tinge.
Six-tenths purity is still not quite the same as seven-tenths.
Five-tenths purity is called a plum-white cake.

Salt-burned cake: two qian and five fen of silver are made into a one-tael piece. Take it out, mix a corrosive brine of rotted salt, spread a layer over the cake, and heat it in the fire; then take it out and hammer off a layer of copper skin. Coat it with the salt mixture and fire it again, then hammer it once more. After repeating this several times, the copper on the surface is gone and the piece turns naturally white—this is called "salt-burned."
What is poured from white copper is what they call "white salt-smelted" silver—a deceptive alloy used to mimic real silver.

The Three-Soldered Cake: The bottom is a full-fineness cake, rolled paper-thin; a core of white metal (lead or tin) is melted inside. For the top, silver is melted in the furnace and poured into fine threads, mixed with two or three qian of lead, then taken out and poured into a charcoal pan to form another very thin cake, placed over the top. The whole is then soldered together, and the four sides are trimmed off. The center is cut through from both sides to hide the seam, making it passable to the untrained eye. To detect it: the cake appears thick; the top and bottom are genuine silver, but the middle shows a different color. Those who know will rub the silver surface on fir wood, revealing three distinct colors at once.

The silver shell is made by turning a piece of silver, creating a hollow cavity. On its surface, which has a fine, pine-grain-like texture, a hole is punched with a pointed tool. Then, a small chisel is used to cut away the interior, removing all the contents and leaving only the silver shell. Lead is poured in to fill the cavity, and a silver point is hammered in to seal it. An iron graver is then used to smooth and finish the surface until it resembles a wind-pot ingot. To identify such counterfeit silver, examine the marks on both sides; they will reveal the truth.

Dao Mao Bing (Fake Silver Cake): First, take top-grade white arsenic and place it in a non-porous crucible sealed with salt mud. Heat it over two sticks of incense beneath a lamp dish; collect the light, clear sublimate for use. Melt seven qian of silver with three qian five fen of copper. Just before removing from the furnace, add seven fen of the arsenic to the silver and cover it. Remove the cast and rub it with arsenic powder: the surface will show chicken-claw marks identical to nine-tenths silver. To distinguish them: genuine nine-tenths silver emerges from the furnace naturally white without rubbing; however, this fake cake's pouring gate shows a yellowish tint, whereas a genuine nine-tenths cake's gate remains white. This distinction makes the deception obvious.

There are also iron-wire cakes, Jiangshan white, Huaguang Bridge, immortal's cake, sprinkled-copper cakes, inverted lead, and dozens of other ingenious fakes that words cannot fully describe. Those who know can reason from one case to the whole: study this and you have grasped more than half. There are idle loafers who will not ply a trade, suffering hardships until they lose their conscience, using this fake silver to scrape together clothes and food and pass their days—these are poor wretches and not worth blaming. But nowadays greedy men whose households are already well off still pass this silver to poison the public, scheming riches for themselves to leave to their sons and grandsons. They do not see that those who deaden their conscience and defy Heaven's principle can have no good reward—how could their descendants prosper? In all dealings among the four classes, only silver of seven-tenths fineness up to pure silk thread should be used; anything lower must not circulate. If you deaden your conscience to cheat others, not only will the debt of unseen punishment be hard to repay—the net of open retribution will not let you slip through.
